title: Incident: Falco reports a shell in the catalog pod, and its token can read Secrets

13:53 Warning: Contact K8S API Server From Container (k8s.ns=shop k8s.pod=catalog-6d9f8b7c4-x2kqp)

14:30: the attacker's next request with the catalog token was refused

objective: Perform behavioral analytics to detect malicious activity with Falco: read and write rules, interpret alerts and identify the Pod and process behind them
secondaryObjectives: Ensure immutability of containers at runtime: read-only root filesystems, no privilege escalation, no exec into production Pods, and recreating rather than patching containers
Use Kubernetes audit logs to monitor access: write an audit Policy with levels per resource and verb, enable it on the API server, and query the log for who did what

sources.note: Read through a summarizing fetch on 2026-11-17 (a third-party page, not Falco's own documentation). Relevant points: the default rule 'Terminal shell in container' at Notice priority, its output fields (user, process, parent, command line, container); custom rules belong in falco_rules.local.yaml because falco_rules.yaml is overwritten on upgrade; readOnlyRootFilesystem blocks runtime changes; a compromised pod is isolated with a quarantine label and a NetworkPolicy that denies all ingress and egress. The page itself deletes the pod without saving evidence; this case follows NIST SP 800-61 on evidence. The 'Contact K8S API Server From Container' rule name and its wording here are to verify against Falco's default rules page (seen only as a search result title on 2026-11-17).

brief.situation: You are the platform security engineer for Pinecrest Outdoor, a fictional online store on Kubernetes. At 14:00 the security channel forwards two Falco alerts from 13:52 and 13:53 on the shop namespace. The catalog service runs image catalog:4.2.0, which the vendor said this morning has a remote code execution flaw. The shop's payment key lives in a Secret in the same namespace.
handover: Falco runs as a DaemonSet in namespace falco; the API server writes an audit log to /var/log/kubernetes/audit/audit.log on cp1.
catalog:4.2.1 fixes the flaw. The team's rule is that production pods are replaced, never patched or entered by hand.
howItWorks: The terminal shows each command's output; the diagram shows the catalog pod, its ServiceAccount and what it can reach.
Each command takes a minute or two; the clock moves only when you act or wait.
When you close, you write the record and explain your reasoning.

source.note: At 14:30 the attacker uses the token again, 30 minutes after the page.

effects.finding: The java process of catalog started a shell that fetched a script from 203.0.113.45, then the container called the API server for the shop Secrets with its own token: the vendor's flaw, exploited.

effects.finding: RoleBinding catalog-reader gives the catalog token get and list on every Secret in shop. catalog needs none of them: its database password comes from a mounted file.

audit.why: Wait for the running command to finish.

effects.finding: At 13:53 the token listed the shop Secrets and read db-password. payments-api-key has not been read yet. db-password must be rotated whatever else happens.

exec.label: kubectl exec -it catalog-6d9f8b7c4-x2kqp -n shop -- sh   (look around inside)

effects.output:
admin@cks-lab:~$ kubectl exec -it catalog-6d9f8b7c4-x2kqp -n shop -- sh
$ ls /tmp
x.sh  kubectl

effects.log: You see the dropped files, but your own shell is now in the evidence: Falco logs your session like the attacker's, and anything you touched is changed.

muteRule.label: Add a falco_rules.local.yaml override: disable 'Terminal shell in container' for namespace shop (too noisy)

effects.output:
admin@cks-lab:~$ kubectl -n falco edit configmap falco-rules-local   # append condition and not k8s.ns.name=shop

effects.log: The alert stops. Nothing else changes.

effects.output:
admin@cks-lab:~$ kubectl delete rolebinding catalog-reader -n shop
rolebinding.rbac.authorization.k8s.io "catalog-reader" deleted

effects.log: The catalog token can no longer read Secrets, from any pod.

harden.label: Roll out catalog:4.2.1 with automountServiceAccountToken: false, runAsNonRoot, readOnlyRootFilesystem and allowPrivilegeEscalation: false

effects.log: New pods run the fixed image, as a non-root user, with a read-only root filesystem and no token{isolated ? "; the quarantined pod is outside the Deployment and stays" : "; the rollout replaced the compromised pod"}.

else.log: 14:30: the catalog token lists and reads every Secret in shop, payments-api-key included.

writeup.question: For the record: what Falco showed, how you contained it, and what you kept.

parts.label: What happened
parts.criteria: Reads the two alerts as one attack: a shell from the java process, then API calls with the pod's own token.
parts.modelAnswer: Falco showed sh spawned by java fetching a script, then the container calling the API for Secrets: the catalog flaw exploited, and the mounted token read db-password at 13:53 (audit log).

parts.label: Contained
parts.criteria: Cuts the token's rights and isolates the pod instead of deleting it, before 14:30.
parts.modelAnswer: Removed RoleBinding catalog-reader so no catalog token can read Secrets, and quarantined the pod with a label and a deny-all NetworkPolicy so it stayed for evidence.

parts.label: Kept and fixed
parts.criteria: Saves evidence before changing anything and without exec, then replaces rather than patches and rotates what was read.
parts.modelAnswer: Saved and hashed the pod spec, logs, Falco and audit entries first; rolled out 4.2.1 with no token, non-root and a read-only root; rotated db-password and payments-api-key.

reasoningCriteria.label: Written why, how and what it cost

expertPath.text: Falco logs: sh from java fetching a script, then API calls for Secrets; the pod's ServiceAccount and labels; can-i shows get and list on Secrets.
The audit log shows db-password read at 13:53; save and hash the pod spec, logs, Falco and audit entries.
Quarantine label and deny-all NetworkPolicy; delete RoleBinding catalog-reader.
Roll out 4.2.1 with no token, non-root and a read-only root; rotate db-password and payments-api-key.

stolen.headline: The token was still good at 14:30
stolen.body: Deleting or isolating the pod is not enough while the ReplicaSet starts a replacement from the same flawed image with the same token. Removing the RoleBinding cuts every copy of the token off from the Secrets at once.

evidenceGone.headline: The evidence went with the pod
evidenceGone.body: A deleted pod takes its logs and filesystem with it. Save the spec, logs, Falco events and audit entries first, then quarantine the pod with a label and a deny-all NetworkPolicy so it stays for analysis.

contained.headline: Good: contained, kept and replaced
contained.body: You read the Falco output fields to the pod and process, checked what the token could do and what the audit log says it did, saved evidence before touching anything, cut the token's rights and isolated the pod, then replaced it hardened and rotated what was read.

gaps.headline: Contained, with gaps
gaps.body: The criteria show what was left: the audit check, an exec that changed the evidence, a muted rule, the hardened rollout or the rotation of the Secret already read.

time_up.headline: Time up
time_up.body: No record was written before the run's hard limit.

scoring.modelReasoning: The 13:52 alert is a shell spawned by java fetching a script from outside: the catalog flaw exploited. The 13:53 alert is the container calling the API server for Secrets with its mounted token, and can-i shows that token can get and list every Secret in shop; the audit log shows it read db-password already. Save and hash the pod spec, logs, Falco events and audit entries before changing anything, and do not exec in. Cut the token off by deleting RoleBinding catalog-reader, and quarantine the pod with a label and a deny-all NetworkPolicy so it stays for analysis. Deleting the pod destroys evidence and the ReplicaSet brings back the same image with the same token. Then roll out the fixed image with no token, non-root and a read-only root filesystem, and rotate the Secrets that were or could have been read. Muting the rule only hides the next attempt.
